You read part of an interview. An analyst asked one future user of a software service a series of questions. You decide, for each question, whether it follows up the answer given just before it.

A question follows up the previous answer when it asks about something that answer said: it asks the speaker to explain, give an example of, say more about, or say why of something the answer mentioned, or it picks up a particular thing the answer named. Wording does not matter; a question can follow up an answer without repeating any of its words.

A question does not follow up the previous answer when it turns to something that answer did not mention, even if the speaker said it in an earlier answer, even if it stays with the same broad subject, and even if it is a good question. A general question that could follow any answer, such as whether there is anything else, does not follow up either.

You receive the pairs of the interview after its first question: for each later question, the answer given just before it, and the question.

Reply with JSON only: an object with one key, "questions", a list with exactly one entry for every pair, in the same order. Each entry has "id", the question's id, and "follow_up", true or false.

Q2
The answer just before it: My daily work involves keeping our drones and charging equipment in working order. I add new drones to our fleet, retire old ones, and set up charging pads at our sites. I also take drones out of service for repairs, put them back, and send them to charge. Regulators can ask us to show how our drones have been looked after.
The question: What attributes and details do you need to record when adding, modifying, or retiring a drone?

Q3
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: What information must be tracked when a drone is taken out of service, repaired, or returned to service, and what must be kept for regulator records?

Q4
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: How do you manage charging pads at sites and what does the service need to do when you send a drone to charge?

Q5
The answer just before it: Each of our company's sites has a few dozen of our own charging pads, and we never lend them to another company. We set up these charging pads at our sites, and we send drones to charge.
The question: Can you tell me what specific actions you perform with drones and charging pads, and what rules or checks the service must enforce?

Q6
The answer just before it: I keep our drones and charging equipment in working order, add new drones to the fleet, retire old ones, and set up charging pads at our sites. I take drones out of service for repairs and put them back, and I send drones to charge. Regulators can ask our company to show how our drones have been looked after.
The question: What records do regulators require your company to show about how drones have been looked after?

Q7
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: Does the charging connector on a charging pad need to match the drone's charging connector?

Q8
The answer just before it: Our drones are of several models from different manufacturers, and they use several connector types that are not interchangeable. Repairs and servicing are carried out by technicians, and regulators can ask a company to show how its drones have been looked after.
The question: Can a drone only charge on its own company's charging pad with a matching connector type?

Q9
The answer just before it: Each company has its own charging pads at its own sites, and pads are never lent to another company. Several connector types are in use and they are not interchangeable.
The question: What states or statuses can a drone have (for example, in service, out of service for repair, charging, retired)?
